addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- graphify: Use for any question about a codebase, its architecture, file relationships, or project content — especially when graphify-out/ exists, where the question should be treated as a graphify query first. Turns any input (code, docs, papers, images, videos) into a persistent knowledge graph with god nodes, community detection, and query/path/explain tools.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

- Python: celery, APScheduler, threading.Timer, asyncio tasks
- Node: setInterval, bull/bullmq, agenda, node-cron
- Any Start() methods on worker/runner types

Search breadth: very thorough. Report file paths and line numbers for everything you find.

---

## Background Workers, Runners, and Scheduling Infrastructure

This is a Go codebase (`github.com/usememos/memos`). Below is every background worker, runner, scheduling mechanism, and async infrastructure found.

---

### 1. SERVER STARTUP AND BACKGROUND RUNNER ORCHESTRATION

**File:** `/bench/home/work/cmd/memos/main.go`
- The `main()` entrypoint (line 214) runs `rootCmd.Execute()`.
- The root command (line 36) creates a `server.Server` and calls `s.Start(ctx)` at line 89.
- A goroutine at line 99 listens for SIGINT/SIGTERM and calls `s.Shutdown(ctx)`.

**File:** `/bench/home/work/server/server.go`
- The `Server` struct (line 31) has fields `backgroundRunnerCancels []context.CancelFunc` and `backgroundRunnerWG sync.WaitGroup` for managing background workers.
- `Server.Start()` (line 101): Starts the HTTP server in a goroutine (line 124), then calls `s.startBackgroundRunners(ctx)` at line 129.
- `Server.startBackgroundRunners()` (line 153): This is the central place where background runners are launched. Currently it starts **only one runner**:
  - **S3 Presign Runner** -- creates `s3presign.NewRunner(s.Store)` at line 162, calls `RunOnce(ctx)` synchronously at line 163 (immediate one-time pass), then launches `s3presignRunner.Run(s3Context)` in a goroutine at lines 167-171 (continuous periodic execution).
- `Server.Shutdown()` (line 134): Calls `stopBackgroundRunners()` (cancels contexts), `closeLongLivedConnections()` (closes SSE hub), `shutdownHTTPServer()`, then `waitBackgroundRunners()` (waits for WaitGroup with timeout).

---

### 2. ACTIVE BACKGROUND RUNNERS

#### 2a. S3 Presign Runner (ACTIVE -- started by server)

**File:** `/bench/home/work/server/runner/s3presign/runner.go`
- `Runner` struct (line 16) holds a `*store.Store`.
- `Run()` (line 29): Uses `time.NewTicker(runnerInterval)` where `runnerInterval = 12 * time.Hour` (line 27). Runs in an infinite loop calling `RunOnce()` every 12 hours, exiting on context cancellation.
- `RunOnce()` (line 43): Calls `CheckAndPresign()`.
- `CheckAndPresign()` (line 47): Iterates through all S3-type attachments in batches of 100, re-presigns URLs for any whose presigned URL will expire within the next day (presigned URLs last 5 days, re-sign after 4 days).
- Started at `/bench/home/work/server/server.go` lines 162-171.

#### 2b. SSE Hub and Heartbeat (ACTIVE -- per-connection)

**File:** `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/sse_hub.go`
- `SSEHub` (line 56): A pub/sub hub managing SSE client connections. Not a background worker per se, but a long-lived concurrent component. Created at `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/v1.go` line 57 via `NewSSEHub()`.
- Closed during shutdown via `s.sseHub.Close()` at `/bench/home/work/server/server.go` line 206.

**File:** `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/sse_handler.go`
- `handleSSE()` (line 34): Each SSE connection spawns a **heartbeat ticker** at line 64 with `time.NewTicker(30 * time.Second)`. This keeps the SSE connection alive by sending `: heartbeat\n\n` every 30 seconds. One ticker per connected client; not a global background worker.

---

### 3. ASYNC DISPATCH WORKERS (init()-started goroutines)

#### 3a. Async Email Workers

**File:** `/bench/home/work/internal/email/email.go`
- In `init()` (line 17): Starts **2 goroutines** that consume from `asyncEmailQueue` (buffered channel of size 128, line 16). Each goroutine loops over the channel, calling `Send()` for each request.
- `SendAsync()` (line 55): Non-blocking enqueue into the channel; drops the email if the queue is full.
- Called via `email.SendAsync` by the notification email dispatcher at `/bench/home/work/server/notification/email.go` line 30.

#### 3b. Async Webhook Workers

**File:** `/bench/home/work/internal/webhook/webhook.go`
- In `init()` (line 42): Starts **4 goroutines** that consume from `asyncPostQueue` (buffered channel of size 128, line 39). Each goroutine loops over the channel, calling `Post()` for each webhook payload.
- `PostAsync()` (line 184): Non-blocking enqueue; drops the payload if the queue is full.
- Called at `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/memo_service_webhooks.go` lines 43 and 71.

---

### 4. CACHE CLEANUP GOROUTINES

**File:** `/bench/home/work/store/cache/cache.go`
- `Cache.cleanupLoop()` (line 200): Each `Cache` instance spawns a goroutine in `New()` (line 83) that uses `time.NewTicker(c.config.CleanupInterval)` (default 5 minutes, per line 62) to periodically evict expired entries.
- `Cache.Close()` (line 187): Signals the goroutine to stop and waits for it to exit.

**File:** `/bench/home/work/store/store.go`
- `Store.New()` (line 38): Creates **3 cache instances**, each spawning its own cleanup goroutine:
  - `instanceSettingCache` (line 51)
  - `userCache` (line 52)
  - `userSettingCache` (line 53)
- `Store.Close()` (line 72): Calls `.Close()` on all three caches, stopping all cleanup goroutines.

So there are **3 background cache cleanup goroutines** running at all times.

---

### 5. FIRE-AND-FORGET GOROUTINES

#### 5a. PAT Usage Recording

**File:** `/bench/home/work/server/auth/authenticator.go`
- `recordPATUsage()` (line 179): Spawns a one-shot goroutine (`go func()` at line 180) each time a Personal Access Token is used, to asynchronously update the `last_used` timestamp in the database.

---

### 6. UNUSED/DORMANT SCHEDULING INFRASTRUCTURE

#### 6a. Internal Scheduler Package (EXISTS BUT IS NOT USED)

**File:** `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/` (entire directory)

This is a complete, production-ready, cron-based job scheduler that is **not imported or used anywhere** in the application code. No file outside `internal/scheduler/` imports it. Key files:

- `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/scheduler.go` -- Full `Scheduler` struct with `Register()`, `Start()`, `Stop()` methods. Launches goroutines per job using `time.NewTimer` to calculate next cron fire time.
- `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/job.go` -- `Job` struct with `Name`, `Schedule` (cron expression), `Timezone`, `Handler`, `Description`, `Tags` fields.
- `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/parser.go` -- Complete cron expression parser supporting 5-field and 6-field formats, with wildcards, ranges, lists, and step values.
- `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/middleware.go` -- `Chain()`, `Recovery()`, `Logging()`, `Timeout()` middleware.
- `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/doc.go` -- Package documentation describing it as "GitHub Actions-inspired cron job scheduler".
- `/bench/home/work/internal/scheduler/README.md` -- Extensive documentation with usage examples.

#### 6b. Memo Payload Runner (EXISTS BUT RUNNER IS NOT USED)

**File:** `/bench/home/work/server/runner/memopayload/runner.go`
- `Runner` struct (line 14) with `RunOnce()` method (line 27) that rebuilds all memo payloads in batches of 100.
- `NewRunner()` (line 19) is **never called** anywhere in the codebase.
- However, the `RebuildMemoPayload()` function (line 74) from this same package IS used inline at `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go` lines 108 and 447, but the Runner wrapper around it is dormant.

---

### SUMMARY TABLE

| Component | Location | Type | Status | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S3 Presign Runner | `server/runner/s3presign/runner.go` | Periodic background runner | **ACTIVE** | `time.NewTicker(12h)` goroutine |
| SSE Hub | `server/router/api/v1/sse_hub.go` | Long-lived pub/sub | **ACTIVE** | Channel-based broadcast |
| SSE Heartbeat | `server/router/api/v1/sse_handler.go:64` | Per-connection ticker | **ACTIVE** | `time.NewTicker(30s)` per client |
| Async Email Workers | `internal/email/email.go:17` | Worker pool | **ACTIVE** | 2 goroutines, buffered channel(128) |
| Async Webhook Workers | `internal/webhook/webhook.go:42` | Worker pool | **ACTIVE** | 4 goroutines, buffered channel(128) |
| Cache Cleanup (x3) | `store/cache/cache.go:83` | Periodic cleanup | **ACTIVE** | `time.NewTicker(5m)` per cache |
| PAT Usage Recording | `server/auth/authenticator.go:180` | Fire-and-forget | **ACTIVE** | One-shot `go func()` per PAT auth |
| Cron Scheduler | `internal/scheduler/` | Cron job scheduler | **UNUSED** | Full cron parser + timer-based scheduling |
| Memo Payload Runner | `server/runner/memopayload/runner.go` | Batch runner | **UNUSED** (Runner wrapper; `RebuildMemoPayload` func used inline) | Batch iteration |

153	func (s *Server) startBackgroundRunners(ctx context.Context) {
154		// Create a separate context for each background runner
155		// This allows us to control cancellation for each runner independently
156		s3Context, s3Cancel := context.WithCancel(ctx)
157	
158		// Store the cancel function so we can properly shut down runners
159		s.backgroundRunnerCancels = append(s.backgroundRunnerCancels, s3Cancel)
160	
161		// Create and start S3 presign runner
162		s3presignRunner := s3presign.NewRunner(s.Store)
163		s3presignRunner.RunOnce(ctx)
164	
165		// Start continuous S3 presign runner
166		s.backgroundRunnerWG.Add(1)
167		go func() {
168			defer s.backgroundRunnerWG.Done()
169			s3presignRunner.Run(s3Context)
170			slog.Info("s3presign runner stopped")
171		}()
172	
173		slog.Info("background runners started")
174	}

176	func (s *Server) stopBackgroundRunners() {
177		for _, cancelFunc := range s.backgroundRunnerCancels {
